frictionVectors.title: EU energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains a major market for Algerian gas, giving Algiers leverage but also exposing it to shifting demand, pricing pressure, and competing LNG suppliers.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya raises border-security costs and complicates Algeria's non-interventionist regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign oil financing
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon production and infrastructure remain heavily dependent on foreign operators and external capital, limiting domestic value capture despite state participation.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked financing and construction remain important for transport and energy projects, creating long-term repayment and strategic-dependence concerns.

highlights: Cotton and minerals under tighter state oversight

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's strategic role depends on trade flows with Nigeria and landlocked neighbors, leaving Benin exposed to border restrictions, customs disputes, and regional political shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the Burkina Faso and Niger borders threatens roads, agricultural zones, and state access to resource-producing areas.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong negotiating power over diamonds, but dependence on global luxury demand and external marketing channels remains a structural vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: New-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, and other critical minerals is increasing, creating pressure to secure local processing and avoid repeating enclave-style extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control struggle
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state control and domestic retention of gold revenues, but informal mining, smuggling, and limited refining capacity constrain sovereignty over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgent disruption
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence threatens mining corridors, transport infrastructure, and rural production, while reliance on external security partnerships introduces new geopolitical dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi Security Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and border activity continue to divert state capacity toward security rather than productive resource governance. Regional mediation remains constrained by distrust.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Aid Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and donors retain significant leverage over mining, energy, and infrastructure decisions. Efforts to increase state oversight are progressing, but transparency and enforcement remain weak.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's ports, exclusive economic zone, and location between Africa, Europe, and the Americas attract competing security and logistics interests. The government must balance partnerships without surrendering strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Tourism Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on tourism, imported energy, and external financing limits economic autonomy during global shocks. Foreign investment is generally regulated, but key infrastructure remains vulnerable to outside market conditions.

highlights: Resource wealth remains state-controlled but opaque

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and contractors remain central to roads, ports, and energy projects, creating long-term bargaining leverage over strategic infrastructure. Debt, procurement opacity, and local-content concerns limit sovereign returns.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Far North Conflicts
frictionVectors.details: Insurgencies continue to disrupt agricultural zones, transport routes, and public investment in the Northwest, Southwest, and Far North. Insecurity raises operating costs and weakens state control over border economies.

highlights: Security partnerships substitute for state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Presence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors retain influence around regime protection and mineral areas, while the state struggles to enforce transparent licensing and revenue collection. The arrangement increases short-term security leverage but reduces institutional autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Weak border control enables armed groups and foreign trading networks to capture value from gold and diamonds. Informal extraction deprives the treasury of revenue and sustains conflict economies.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the sovereignty anchor

frictionVectors.title: Oil Infrastructure and Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon exports provide essential fiscal leverage but remain exposed to foreign operators, external markets, and transit infrastructure. Limited diversification leaves national bargaining power vulnerable to price and production shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Sudan Border Pressures
frictionVectors.details: Conflict spillovers, refugee flows, and armed-group activity along the western and eastern borders force continued reliance on foreign military and diplomatic partners. Security imperatives often override civilian oversight of strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a longstanding sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros's effective control over surrounding maritime and migration routes.

frictionVectors.title: External aid dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and energy projects remain heavily dependent on Gulf, French, and multilateral financing, narrowing domestic policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern armed conflict
frictionVectors.details: M23-linked territorial advances and regional interference continue to undermine Kinshasa's authority in the east and threaten transport corridors near strategic mineral zones.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain major influence across copper and cobalt value chains, while Western and Gulf actors seek greater access without materially shifting local refining capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state's fiscal position remains tightly tied to offshore oil, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price swings, production agreements, and foreign technical operators.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and port projects expand connectivity but preserve significant external leverage over strategic infrastructure and future revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is increasing domestic processing, but foreign traders, financiers, and manufacturers still capture substantial value from the cocoa economy.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist spillover from the Sahel continues to drive reliance on foreign intelligence, equipment, and regional security partnerships along the northern frontier.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: American, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue but constrain strategic maneuver and expose Djibouti to great-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: China-linked port and rail financing has strengthened logistics capacity while increasing concerns over debt dependence and external influence over critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: External financing from Gulf partners and the IMF is supporting fiscal stability but increases outside influence over major real-estate, port, and infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Suez revenues remain vulnerable to Red Sea insecurity, while Nile water tensions with Ethiopia constrain Egypt's strategic freedom and resource security.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining or volatile oil and gas output limits fiscal room and leaves the state dependent on foreign energy firms, markets, and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Port Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure has improved connectivity but can narrow sovereign discretion through financing, contractor, and repayment dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper, gold, and other mineral projects rely heavily on foreign capital and expertise, creating persistent tensions over revenue capture, labor conditions, and control.

frictionVectors.title: Militarized Regional Access
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's strategic Red Sea location attracts competing regional powers, while border tensions and limited transparency heighten the risk that infrastructure serves external security agendas.

frictionVectors.title: Cross-Border Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, energy, transport, and investment ties with South Africa provide essential resilience but limit Eswatini's room for independent economic and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and Forestry Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Export agriculture and forestry remain vulnerable to external market rules, water constraints, and multinational value chains that capture much of the higher-value processing.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam enhances domestic power capacity and bargaining leverage, but unresolved arrangements with Egypt and Sudan remain a major regional flashpoint.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked Ethiopia's need for reliable corridors through Djibouti and other coastal routes exposes it to foreign leverage, while debt restructuring constrains infrastructure choices.

highlights: Oil and manganese remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater domestic participation and fiscal returns from oil, manganese, and infrastructure concessions. Policy uncertainty remains a concern for established foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon requires foreign capital and technical partners for transport, energy, and extractive projects, creating leverage for Gulf, Chinese, and Western investors.

highlights: Senegal remains the critical strategic partner

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic influence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, energy links, security cooperation, and access through Senegal shape Gambia's strategic autonomy. Border and fisheries-management disputes periodically expose this dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and port vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic energy capacity and dependence on imported fuel constrain sovereign control over economic infrastructure. Port modernization also relies heavily on external financing and operators.

highlights: Gold remains the primary sovereignty asset

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector leakage and illicit mining
frictionVectors.details: Illegal and informal mining weakens environmental governance, reduces state revenue, and enables foreign-linked trading networks to capture value outside formal channels.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt-restructuring obligations and IMF conditionality limit fiscal flexibility over energy, mining, and industrial policy. Chinese and other external infrastructure financing remains strategically important.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project is drawing intense Chinese, Western, and regional competition over rail, port, and processing infrastructure. Guinea's ability to convert the project into broad domestic value remains uncertain.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on foreign mining firms and export corridors leaves the economy exposed to external pricing, logistics, and political leverage. The authorities continue pressing for local processing and higher state participation.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Most cashew value is exported with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and state revenues vulnerable to foreign buyers, price swings, and informal trade networks.

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port and security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political tensions make the port, fisheries, and transport sectors vulnerable to outside influence. Drug-trafficking networks further erode state control and complicate international security involvement.

highlights: Ports and power remain strategic battlegrounds

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL DEBT AND INFRASTRUCTURE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and lender conditions constrain Nairobi's room to manage transport and energy assets on purely national terms. Chinese-built infrastructure and Western financial oversight remain complementary but competing channels of influence.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the LAPSSET corridor are central to regional trade and security. Foreign operators, Gulf investors, and neighboring states all seek influence over logistics infrastructure and associated land corridors.

highlights: Water sovereignty rests on South African demand

frictionVectors.title: LESOTHO HIGHLANDS WATER PROJECT
frictionVectors.details: Water transfers to South Africa provide essential revenue but leave Lesotho structurally dependent on a dominant neighbor for financing, markets, and infrastructure. Delays, compensation disputes, and project governance remain recurring sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: TEXTILE AND LABOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The export garment sector relies heavily on foreign manufacturers and preferential market access. External firms can shift production quickly, limiting domestic value capture and exposing the country to changing trade rules.

highlights: Ports remain central to sovereign control

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE CONCESSIONS AND RAIL ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Large iron ore projects and access to rail and port infrastructure create significant foreign leverage over Liberia's export economy. The core challenge is converting concession activity into durable public revenue, local processing, and infrastructure ownership.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and investors remain important to port modernization, shipping, and Liberia's maritime registry. Weak bargaining capacity can leave the state carrying security and maintenance costs while external actors capture a disproportionate share of value.

highlights: Foreign security patrons shape infrastructure access

frictionVectors.title: COMPETING CONTROL OF OIL ASSETS
frictionVectors.details: Rival authorities and armed networks continue to contest budget flows, terminals, and production decisions through the national oil system. Foreign commercial and political patrons amplify fragmentation and complicate transparent revenue management.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN MILITARY AND ENERGY FOOTPRINTS
frictionVectors.details: External military support, contractors, and energy interests remain embedded in Libya's security landscape. This increases the risk that ports, pipelines, and reconstruction contracts serve geopolitical patrons before national infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Mining exports outpace domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: NICKEL, COBALT, AND MINERAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining projects provide exports and jobs but leave Madagascar exposed to commodity prices, imported inputs, and limited local processing. Fiscal terms and environmental disputes continue to test the state's ability to retain value.

frictionVectors.title: LAND, FORESTS, AND FOREIGN INVESTMENT
frictionVectors.details: Agricultural, conservation, and infrastructure projects can generate conflict over land rights and resource access. Weak enforcement enables illegal logging and informal extraction, reducing national control over strategic ecological assets.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms constrain policy space, while fuel, fertilizer, and foreign-exchange shortages expose Malawi to external supply pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Renewed interest in uranium, rare earths, and other minerals could diversify revenue, but weak bargaining capacity and regulatory enforcement risk disproportionate foreign capture.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The military government relies heavily on Russian security support, reducing Western leverage but creating new dependency and opaque costs around strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to raise the state's share of gold revenues have improved fiscal claims but intensified disputes with foreign operators and increased uncertainty for future investment.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project strengthens Mauritania's export position, but dependence on foreign operators, offshore infrastructure, and Senegalese coordination limits unilateral control.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Corridor Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and proposed green-hydrogen projects attract Gulf, European, and Asian capital; port and transmission investments could deepen growth while locking in external ownership of logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Transition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to negotiations involving the United Kingdom and the Diego Garcia military facility, limiting full control over maritime assets.

frictionVectors.title: Financial and Maritime Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to external financial regulation, tourism cycles, and imported energy, even as Mauritius seeks greater value from ocean resources and regional connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Politics
frictionVectors.details: Control and development of Western Sahara underpin Morocco's strategic position but remain contested internationally, creating legal and diplomatic risk around fisheries, phosphates, and renewables.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital Balancing
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and U.S. investment supports ports, energy, and industrial expansion, but competition among partners requires careful protection of Moroccan ownership and policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique's liquefied natural gas ambitions remain heavily dependent on foreign operators, financiers, and security guarantees. Delays and renegotiations limit Maputo's near-term control over revenues and project timing.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Gap
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten gas infrastructure and population displacement despite government, regional, and external military support. Security reliance on partners constrains sovereign freedom of action.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital Leverage
frictionVectors.details: New oil, uranium, lithium, and green-hydrogen projects require substantial foreign investment and technical expertise. Namibia is seeking stronger local participation and fiscal terms to prevent renewed enclave-style extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Ports, electricity transmission, water supply, and transport capacity could constrain the government's ability to capture value from expanding resource projects. Regional logistics dependence remains significant.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Oil Reconfiguration
frictionVectors.details: The junta is renegotiating mining and energy relationships to increase state control while reducing French and Western influence. Weak institutional capacity and sanctions-related disruption could nevertheless reduce realized national revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Security and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger increasingly relies on Russian security cooperation and regional alternatives for trade and energy access. Persistent jihadist attacks and fragile transport corridors limit effective control beyond major urban centers.

highlights: Gas and Grid Security Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy and Finance Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies, creditors, traders, and contractors remain central to Nigeria's hydrocarbon sector. Reform efforts aim to attract investment, but financing and technology dependence continue to dilute domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Grid Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, sabotage, insurgency, and unreliable electricity infrastructure undermine production and industrial sovereignty. The state retains formal ownership while losing substantial value through operational failures and leakage.

highlights: Tight State Control of Strategic Assets

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern DRC generate diplomatic, sanctions, and reputational pressure. The dispute threatens access to Western partnerships even as Kigali maintains strong internal control.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda exercises substantial policy control but remains dependent on foreign aid, concessional finance, and external investment for infrastructure and growth. Potential donor conditionality is increasing as regional tensions persist.

highlights: Gulf of Guinea maritime vigilance rises

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Exploration Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International firms and neighboring states retain significant influence over prospective offshore blocks, while commercial discoveries remain uncertain. São Tomé and Príncipe has limited fiscal and technical capacity to shape exploration terms alone.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country's strategic location gives it value for Gulf of Guinea surveillance, but maritime enforcement depends heavily on external partners and regional cooperation.

highlights: New oil and gas era tests national control

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Operator Dominance
frictionVectors.details: International companies remain central to developing offshore oil and gas projects, creating pressure for stronger local-content rules, contract transparency, and a larger domestic share of revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Nationalism Versus Financing
frictionVectors.details: Government efforts to review contracts and increase state participation may improve sovereignty but could complicate relations with lenders, investors, and existing project partners.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Maritime Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on outside partners, including India and other international actors, for maritime surveillance, coastal security, and port-related capabilities. This support strengthens enforcement but can narrow policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Tourism Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on tourism, imported goods, and climate-sensitive infrastructure leaves the country vulnerable to external financing conditions and shocks despite progress in fisheries and blue-economy governance.

highlights: Iron ore wealth meets fiscal fragility

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore and mineral projects are primarily financed and operated by foreign companies, limiting domestic value capture and increasing disputes over taxation, concessions, and local benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Resources Risk
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, and power needs encourage government reliance on external investors and lenders. Weak bargaining capacity can leave infrastructure arrangements tilted toward exporters rather than broad industrialization.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Port Agendas
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and neighboring countries pursue overlapping security and port interests, while federal and regional authorities do not always align. This fragments control over strategic infrastructure and maritime revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence and Resource Access
frictionVectors.details: International military support remains essential against al-Shabaab and for protecting shipping, fisheries, and offshore prospects. Dependence on external security providers limits the state's ability to set and enforce unified resource rules.

frictionVectors.title: RAIL, PORT AND LOGISTICS BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Chronic failures at Transnet-linked railways and ports constrain mineral exports and weaken Pretoria's practical control over strategic supply chains. Public-private reforms are advancing, but implementation remains vulnerable to entrenched interests and foreign capital dependence.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for preferential access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and other minerals. South Africa retains policy autonomy but faces pressure to align standards, processing rules, and security cooperation with competing blocs.

frictionVectors.title: OIL EXPORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's fiscal survival depends on oil transported through Sudanese infrastructure, leaving revenue flows exposed to war, transit disruptions, and opaque contracting. External firms and neighboring states retain significant leverage over production, marketing, and export access.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and renewed fighting risks draw in Uganda, Sudan-linked networks, and international humanitarian and security actors. Weak state institutions limit Juba's ability to secure transport corridors and regulate resource zones independently.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Competing military and commercial networks use gold production and smuggling to finance operations, while foreign actors seek access through security, trade, and political channels. The conflict has sharply reduced civilian and national institutional control over mining regions.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND AGRICULTURAL CORRIDORS
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, Red Sea access, and major transport routes has become strategically contested. External logistical, financial, and military support to rival factions increases the risk that infrastructure and export routes serve foreign-backed war economies rather than national recovery.

frictionVectors.title: RAIL AND PORT FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and Western-linked capital is competing around railways, ports, and logistics corridors, including routes connected to inland neighbors. Dodoma is widening its options, but debt exposure and concession terms remain important sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater local processing, fiscal returns, and oversight of gold and critical-mineral projects. Negotiations with multinational firms and investor-state concerns could still constrain Tanzania's ability to fully capture downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRANSIT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé remains a vital commercial gateway for landlocked Sahel markets, attracting foreign operators and strategic investment. This creates revenue and diplomatic leverage but also exposes Togo to external pressure over customs, logistics, and sanctions-sensitive trade.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence and instability moving south from Burkina Faso threaten northern transport corridors and state presence. Togo is expanding regional security cooperation, but reliance on outside training, intelligence, and equipment limits fully independent security control.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Financing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: European funding and trade access remain linked to migration control, giving Brussels leverage over Tunisian policy while domestic resistance to external conditions grows.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Electricity Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on imported energy and Algerian gas, constraining strategic autonomy as fiscal stress limits investment in domestic production and renewables.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Risk
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline strengthens future export capacity but remains exposed to Western environmental campaigns, financing constraints, and reputational pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain central to transport and energy projects, expanding Uganda's infrastructure options while increasing long-term dependence on external capital and repayment flows.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership and Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Government efforts to secure greater domestic benefit from copper and critical-mineral production face resistance from multinational operators and dependence on foreign technology and capital.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has reduced immediate fiscal pressure, but Chinese, Western, and multilateral financing still shapes infrastructure priorities and limits room for unilateral policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Control
frictionVectors.details: Export restrictions and local-processing demands seek to retain more lithium and platinum value domestically, but Chinese-linked firms remain prominent in extraction, refining, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Sanctions Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, arrears, and limited access to international capital keep Zimbabwe reliant on opaque bilateral financing and commodity-backed arrangements, weakening sovereign bargaining power.
